nameStory: This lichen gets its "toadskin" name from its bumpy, warty surface that looks remarkably like the rough, pebbly skin of a toad. The "Pennsylvania" part comes from where it was first scientifically described, though it's found throughout northeastern North America. Early naturalists thought these crusty, leather-like patches clinging to rocks looked so much like amphibian skin that the name stuck!
description: Pennsylvania Toadskin Lichen is a crusty, brownish-gray lichen that forms circular patches on rock surfaces. It's actually a partnership between a fungus and algae working together - the fungus provides structure while the algae make food through photosynthesis. These patches can grow 2-6 inches across and have a distinctly bumpy, warty texture that feels rough to the touch. When dry, it appears grayish-brown and brittle, but when wet it becomes darker and slightly more flexible.

idTips.label: Warty, bumpy surface
idTips.description: The top surface is covered in small, raised bumps and warts that feel rough like sandpaper when you run your finger across it

idTips.label: Single attachment point
idTips.description: The entire circular patch attaches to the rock at just one central point underneath, like a belly button - you can often lift the edges slightly

idTips.label: Circular growth pattern
idTips.description: Forms roughly round patches that expand outward from the center, often with slightly wavy or lobed edges

idTips.label: Color changes when wet
idTips.description: Dry patches appear light grayish-brown, but turn much darker brown or nearly black when wet from rain

idTips.label: Brittle texture when dry
idTips.description: Feels stiff and papery when dry - you might hear a slight crackling sound if you gently press on it

habitat: Look for Pennsylvania Toadskin Lichen on exposed rock faces and boulders in New England's mountains and hills, particularly on acidic rocks like granite and quartzite. It thrives on vertical or slanted rock surfaces that get good air circulation but aren't constantly wet. You'll often find it in areas above 1,000 feet elevation, from the White Mountains down through the Berkshires.

seasonality.spring: Becomes more active as temperatures warm and spring rains provide moisture. This is when you'll see the most dramatic color changes from wet to dry.
seasonality.summer: Often appears grayish and dried out during hot, dry periods. Look for it on north-facing rocks or in shaded areas where it stays slightly more hydrated.
seasonality.fall: Excellent time for observation as cool, moist weather keeps it hydrated and darker colored. Fall rains make the warty texture especially pronounced.
seasonality.winter: Remains visible on snow-free rock faces. The lichen goes dormant but doesn't disappear - look for the distinctive circular patches on exposed cliff faces.

funFact: This lichen can literally come back from the dead - it can lose up to 95% of its water content and become completely brittle and dormant, then spring back to life within minutes of getting wet again, resuming photosynthesis almost instantly!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with Common Toadskin Lichen, but Pennsylvania Toadskin has much more pronounced bumps and warts on its surface. Memory trick: Pennsylvania Toadskin is like a toad with really bad acne - the bumps are much more obvious and raised than its smoother cousin.
contextualKnowledge: The word 'lichen' is pronounced 'LIE-ken' by most botanists, though 'LICH-en' is also acceptable. Many people don't realize that lichens aren't plants at all - they're actually a fungus and algae living together in a mutually beneficial partnership called symbiosis.
compareHints: Pennsylvania Toadskin Lichen differs from Common Toadskin Lichen by having much more prominent surface bumps and warts - the texture is significantly rougher and more pronounced. While both attach at a single central point, Pennsylvania Toadskin's warty surface makes it look like it has a skin condition compared to the relatively smoother Common Toadskin. Pennsylvania Toadskin also tends to be found at slightly higher elevations and on more exposed rock faces.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Common Toadskin Lichen differs from its close relative Pennsylvania Toadskin Lichen by having more pronounced bumps and blisters on its surface, giving it a more dramatically textured appearance.
